grammar.title: Present perfect simple and continuous
grammar.short: Experiences, results and actions that continue

slides.hook: Have you ever earned your own money? How long have you been saving for something special?

rows: She has set up a company.
She has been running it for a year.
We haven't made a profit yet.
Have you opened a bank account?
How long have you been saving?

p: Use it for experiences (ever / never), results we can see now, and actions with 'already', 'just' and 'yet'.
It answers: How many? How much?
ex: Have you **ever set up** a business?
Lola **has made** a profit of 200 euros this month.
I**'ve** just **opened** my first bank account.

p: Use it for actions that started in the past and are still happening, or have just stopped and we can see the effects.
It answers: How long? It focuses on the activity.
ex: Marco **has been running** his online shop since 2023.
I'm exhausted because I**'ve been working** on my business plan.
How long **have** you **been saving** for a laptop?

rows: I've had my bank account for two years.
I've had my bank account since 2024.
She's been earning wages for six months.
She's been earning wages since June.
They've been entrepreneurs since they were fifteen.
She has earned 500 euros in wages.
She has been working at the café all summer.
slides.note: State verbs (know, like, have = own, believe) only use the simple: I've known my business partner for years.

slides.title: Meet Ana, 16, entrepreneur
text: Ana **has been making** jewellery since she was twelve. Two years ago she **set up** an online shop, and since then she **has sold** more than 1,000 bracelets.
'I**'ve been working** really hard,' she says. 'My expenses are low, so I**'ve made** a good profit. I**'ve** already **saved** enough for a new laptop!'
Her secret? Creativity, time management and great communication skills.

items: I've been knowing my business partner since 2020.
I've known my business partner since 2020.
I run this shop for five years.
I've run / I've been running this shop for five years.
The situation continues up to now → present perfect.
I've been selling 50 T-shirts this week.
A number of completed things → simple.

slides.q: She ___ cupcakes since 9 a.m. for her new business – the kitchen smells amazing!
slides.e: Focus on the activity and how long; we can see (and smell!) the effects.

slides.q: Our company ___ a profit of 1,000 euros so far.

p: Simple → result, experience, how many / how much.
Continuous → activity in progress, how long.
for + a period; since + a starting point.

grammar.title: Question forms
grammar.short: Subject and object questions, indirect questions

slides.hook: What questions do people ask in a job interview? Which personal skills would you talk about?

slides.note: Remember QUASI: Question word – Auxiliary – Subject – Infinitive.

p: When the question word (who, what, which) is the SUBJECT, we don't use do / does / did. The word order is the same as a statement.
ex: **Who runs** the company? (Somebody runs the company.)

rows: Who paid the entrepreneur?  (The bank paid her.)
Who did the entrepreneur pay?  (She paid her workers.)
What made a profit?  (The café made a profit.)
What did you buy with your wages?

p: Indirect questions are more polite – perfect for interviews! Start with 'Could you tell me...', 'Do you know...', 'I'd like to know...'. Then use statement word order (no do/does/did).
ex: Could you tell me **where the nearest cash machine is**?
Do you know **how much the bank charges**?
I'd like to know **if you have leadership skills**.

slides.title: A summer job at the café
text: Manager: So, **what do you do** in your free time?
Leo: I design websites. I'm good at computer programming and I have good organizational skills.
Manager: Great. **Have you ever worked** with money?
Leo: Yes, I help at my aunt's shop. Could you tell me **what the wages are**? And I'd like to know **whether I can work** at weekends.
Manager: Of course. **Who told** you about this job?

items: Could you tell me where is the cash machine?
Could you tell me where the cash machine is?

slides.e: 'Who' is the subject, so no auxiliary.

p: Object questions: QW + auxiliary + subject + verb.
Subject questions: who / what + verb (no do / did).
Indirect questions: polite phrase + statement order.
Yes/no indirect questions use if / whether.
